# Judith Chapter 16 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Judith 16

---

## THE SONG OF JUDITH (vv. 1–17)

**1** And Judith said:

Strike up to my God with timbrels,
    sing to my Lord with cymbals;
sound for him a new psalm,
    exalt him and call upon his name.

**2** For the LORD is a God who crushes wars;
    he has pitched his camp among his people;
    he delivered me from the hand of those who pursued me.

**3** Assur came from the mountains of the north,
    he came with ten thousands of his army;
their multitude choked the wadis,
    and their cavalry covered the hills.

**4** He declared he would set fire to my territory
    and put my young men to the sword,
    and dash my infants against the ground,
    and give my children up as plunder,
    and take my virgins as spoil.

**5** But the Lord Almighty brought them to nothing
    by the hand of a woman.

**6** For their champion fell not by the hand of young men,
    nor did the sons of Titans cut him down,
    nor did tall giants fall upon him;
but Judith daughter of Merari
    undid him with the beauty of her face.

**7** For she put off the garb of her widowhood
    to exalt the afflicted in Israel;
she anointed her face with precious oil,

**8** she bound her hair in a tiara,
    and put on a linen garment to deceive him.

**9** Her sandal ravished his eye,
    her beauty captured his soul —
    and the sword passed through his neck.

**10** The Persians trembled at her audacity,
    the Medes were confounded by her daring.

**11** Then my wretched ones raised a shout
    and my weak ones cried out;
the enemy was terror-stricken, they shrieked and fled.

**12** Sons of girls pierced them through,
    and like deserters' children wounded them;
they fell before the face of the LORD my God.

**13** I will sing to my God a new song:
O Lord, you are great and glorious,
    wondrous in strength, unconquerable.

**14** Let all your creation serve you,
    for you spoke and they came to be;
you sent forth your breath and it fashioned them;
    and none can resist your voice.

**15** For mountains shall be shaken to their foundations along with the waters,
    and rocks shall melt before your face like wax;
but to those who fear you
    you will still show mercy.

**16** For a fragrant offering is a small thing,
    and the fat of whole burnt offerings is less than nothing to you;
but whoever fears the Lord shall be great forever.

**17** Woe to the nations that rise against my people —
    the Lord Almighty will punish them on the day of judgment;
he will send fire and worms into their flesh,
    and they will weep in pain forever.

---

**18** When they came to Jerusalem, they worshiped God. When the people had been purified, they offered their whole burnt offerings, their freewill offerings, and their gifts.

**19** Judith dedicated to God all the possessions of Holofernes that the people had given her; and the canopy she had taken from his bedchamber she gave as a devoted thing to God.

**20** The people continued in festival before the sanctuary in Jerusalem for three months, and Judith remained with them.

**21** After these days every man went to his own inheritance, and Judith went to Bethulia and remained on her estate. For the rest of her life she was honored throughout all the land of Israel.

**22** Many men desired her, but no man knew her all the days of her life, from the day her husband Manasseh died and was gathered to his people.

**23** She grew even more renowned and she grew old in the house of her husband, living to one hundred and five years. She set her maidservant free. And she died in Bethulia, and they buried her in the cave of her husband Manasseh.

**24** The house of Israel mourned her for seven days. Before her death she distributed her property to those nearest to her husband Manasseh and to those nearest to her own family.

**25** And no one ever again spread terror among the sons of Israel in the days of Judith, nor for a long time after her death.

---

### Council Notes

**On verse 1 — "new psalm" vs. "new song":** EMET uses "new psalm" (Greek psalmon kainon), LOGOS "new psalm," PNEUMA "new song." The Greek psalmos is properly a psalm/song sung to an instrument. "New psalm" is more accurate; "new song" is the more common biblical phrase (Ps 96:1; 98:1; Isa 42:10). SOPHIA uses "new psalm" to distinguish this from those Psalter compositions while noting the echo.

**On verse 2 — "crushes wars" vs. "shatters wars":** EMET/LOGOS: "crushes wars." PNEUMA: "shatters wars." Greek syntribōn polemos — "crushing/breaking wars." Both work; SOPHIA retains "crushes" as the traditional rendering of this divine epithet (echoing Exodus 15:3: "The LORD is a man of war").

**On verse 5 — "woman" vs. "female":** This is the most theologically charged lexical choice in the chapter. Greek thēleia is the adjective meaning "female" — the same word used of female animals. It is not the usual word for woman (gynē). EMET renders it "female" to preserve the pointed usage. LOGOS renders "woman." SOPHIA ruling: "woman" — the pointed category-word in English is "woman," and the context makes the force clear. "Female" in English can sound clinical or reductive in a way Greek thēleia does not.

**On verse 6 — "sons of Titans":** All agents preserve "Titans" (Titanes). This is a Hellenistic reference to the supreme mythological power — not "giants" (which appears separately as the next term). The author deliberately invokes the highest categories of human and mythological force to say none of them could do what Judith did. The reference must be preserved, not smoothed to "mighty men."

**On verse 9 — sequence of the three clauses:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA all render the three-part verse (sandal/eye, beauty/soul, sword/neck) in the same order. The verse is a masterpiece of compressed narrative: three beats that contain the entire story in miniature. SOPHIA retains the exact sequence and syntax.

**On verse 14 — "breath" vs. "spirit":** Greek pneuma — the word can mean breath, wind, or spirit. In the context of creation (you spoke → you breathed → they came to be), the parallel with Genesis 2:7 and Psalm 104:30 is explicit. LOGOS renders "spirit" (divine agency); EMET/PNEUMA render "breath" (physical act). SOPHIA uses "breath" to preserve the creation-imagery and let the reader hear the Genesis echo.

**On verse 16 — the theology of fear vs. sacrifice:** This verse is a direct statement of a major biblical theme: formal sacrifice is inferior to the fear of God. It echoes 1 Samuel 15:22, Psalm 51:16-17, Hosea 6:6, Amos 5:21-24. The book of Judith is making a theological claim: what Judith did — her courage rooted in fear of God — surpasses any temple offering.

**On verse 25 — THE EPITAPH:**

All three agents render this verse. The differences are minor. The content is everything.

- EMET: "no one ever spread fear among the sons of Israel again in the days of Judith, and for many days after her death"
- LOGOS: "no one ever again spread terror among the sons of Israel in the days of Judith, nor for a long time after her death"
- PNEUMA: "no one ever again spread terror among the sons of Israel — not in the days of Judith, and not for a long time after she was gone"

**SOPHIA ruling:** "And no one ever again spread terror among the sons of Israel in the days of Judith, nor for a long time after her death."

The verse stands alone. It is the final sentence of the Book of Judith. It is not a triumphant shout but a quiet statement of what her life meant: the absence of fear. Peace as legacy. The book began with a world-conqueror who spread terror across nations. It ends with a widow from a small city who ended that terror, and whose legacy was measured not in conquest but in safety — the safety of a people who lived without fear because of what she did. The silence after this sentence is the monument.
